title: A simple rational module of a split semisimple group has a multiplicity-one torus weight
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme] which is semisimple, meaning that after algebraic closure it has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup; solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes become trivial. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq G$: a closed subgroup isomorphic over $k$ to a finite product of $\mathbf G_m$, maximal among tori after algebraic closure, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$. Let $V\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional rational $G$-representation [def-wf-algebraic-representations]. A rational subrepresentation is a $k$-linear subspace preserved by $G(A)$ after extension to every commutative $k$-algebra $A$; simple means that the only such subspaces are $0$ and $V$. Assume that $V$ is simple. For a character $\lambda:T\to\mathbf G_m$, define
$$V_\lambda=\{v\in V: t(1\otimes v)=\lambda(t)(1\otimes v)\text{ in }A\otimes_kV\text{ for every commutative }k\text{-algebra }A\text{ and every }t\in T(A)\}.$$
There exists a character $\lambda:T\to\mathbf G_m$ for which $\dim_k V_\lambda=1$. The field $k$ need not be algebraically closed or of characteristic zero, and $G$ need not be simply connected.

source.place: Theorem 22.2, printed pp.463--464 (multiplicity-one weight for every simple module of a split reductive group); Theorem 22.18(b), printed p.467. Semisimple is a special case of reductive, Chapter 19a--19b.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-borel-pair] to the given $G,T$. The group $G$ is smooth, connected, affine, of finite type and geometrically semisimple, and $T$ is a split torus maximal after algebraic closure, as required. Obtain $B,U,p$ with $B=U\rtimes T$ and $B$ smooth connected affine, of finite type and split solvable. Apply [lem-sfb-split-solvable-triangular-embedding] to $B$ to get a closed immersion $B\hookrightarrow B_n$ over $k$. Restrict the rational representation $V$ to $B$. The coaction dictionary [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary] identifies this restriction with a finite-dimensional rational $B$-comodule. Since $V\ne0$, [lem-sfb-triangular-group-representation-eigenline] gives a line $L\subseteq V$ and a character $\chi:B\to\mathbf G_m$ acting on $L$ after every algebra extension. Choose $0\ne v\in L$.

source.place: Theorem 22.18, first two sentences of the proof, printed p.467; splitness from 21.34 and trigonalizability from 16.52.

proof.text: Put $\lambda=\chi|_T$. The target $\mathbf G_m$ is of multiplicative type, being a rank-one split torus. The unipotent-to-multiplicative result [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial] applied to $\chi|_U$ says that it is trivial on every algebra. Thus for $b=ut\in B(A)$ one has $\chi(b)=\chi(u)\chi(t)=\lambda(t)=\lambda(p(b))$. Consequently $v$ is a primitive vector in precisely the form needed by the cyclic weight bound: $b(1\otimes v)=\lambda(p(b))(1\otimes v)$ on every commutative $k$-algebra $A$.

source.place: Definition 22.16 and Theorem 22.18, printed p.467; Proposition 14.18, triviality of unipotent characters.

proof.text: Use the coaction dictionary [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary] to write $c:V\to V\otimes_k C$, $C=k[G]$. Fix a $k$-basis $(a_i)$ of $C$ and write $c(x)=\sum_i c_i(x)\otimes a_i$, with finitely many terms for each $x$. A subspace $W$ is a rational submodule exactly when $c_i(W)\subseteq W$ for every $i$: one implication evaluates at the universal point, and the other evaluates this formula at arbitrary algebra-valued points. Starting with $W_0=kv$, define $W_{j+1}=W_j+\sum_i c_i(W_j)$. Finite dimension makes this increasing sequence stabilize. Its stable value is a nonzero rational submodule, hence is $V$ by simplicity. For any field extension $F/k$, $(1\otimes a_i)$ is an $F$-basis of $F\otimes_k C$, and the coefficient operators are $1\otimes c_i$. Induction gives the corresponding sequence $F\otimes_k W_j$. It too reaches $V_F$. Therefore $v_F=1\otimes v$ generates $V_F$ as a rational $G_F$-module; no assertion of simplicity after extension was used.

source.place: Theorem 22.18, printed p.467: simplicity makes the primitive vector cyclic. Elementary coefficient-span calculation supplies cyclic generation after scalar extension, without using 22.4.

proof.text: Choose an algebraic closure $F/k$ using [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. The structural node [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-borel-pair] ensures that $B_F$ is a Borel, $U_F$ its unipotent radical, and $B_F=U_F\rtimes T_F$ with projection $p_F$. The group $G_F$ is smooth, affine and of finite type, since $k[G]\to F\otimes_kk[G]$ is a base change of a smooth ring map [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-base-change-composition]; it is connected by [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected], applied to the connected $k$-scheme $G$ with the identity section as rational point. Hence $G_F$ is semisimple by hypothesis, and reductive by the last assertion of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Apply [lem-sfb-primitive-cyclic-weight-bound] to $G_F,T_F,B_F,V_F,v_F,\lambda_F$. Its primitive-vector equality is step 2 after extension; $v_F\ne0$ by extending a basis containing $v$; finite dimension and cyclic generation are step 3. Its conclusion gives $(V_F)_{\lambda_F}=Fv_F$. In particular this character space has dimension one over $F$.

source.place: Proposition 22.17, printed p.467, applied over an algebraic closure to the same cyclic primitive representation; only its multiplicity-one conclusion is used.

proof.text: Choose $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$. A character function in $k[\mathbf Z^r]$ is a monomial $e^m$: in the equations $\Delta(f)=f\otimes f$, $\epsilon(f)=1$, comparison of pairs of distinct monomials leaves just one nonzero coefficient, which equals $1$. By the coaction dictionary, the weight space in the item is the coaction eigenspace $c_T(x)=x\otimes e^m$: evaluate at the universal point for one direction and at any point for the other. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-torus-bundle-weights] with $A=k$, $A'=F$ and this $m$. The finite-dimensional space $V$ is finite free, so its projectivity hypothesis holds. It identifies $F\otimes_k V_\lambda$ with $(V_F)_{\lambda_F}$. A $k$-basis of $V_\lambda$ becomes an $F$-basis of its scalar extension. Step 4 therefore gives $\dim_k V_\lambda=1$, for the character $\lambda$ already defined over $k$ in step 2.

source.place: Theorem 12.12, printed pp.234--235, character-space decomposition and its elementary scalar-extension form; descent of the multiplicity-one conclusion of 22.18(b).

proof_origin.place: Theorem 22.18 and Proposition 22.17, p.467. Follows the source primitive-vector route; reuses the algebraically closed cyclic-weight node via an explicit coefficient-span scalar-extension calculation rather than duplicating it over arbitrary fields.
